Now I have all the information I need. Let me provide you with the complete list.

## U.S. Secretaries of Health and Human Services — 2018 to End of 2024

Here is every individual who served (as appointed or acting) in the HHS Secretary role from the beginning of 2018 through December 31, 2024:

---

### 1. **Alex Azar** *(24th Secretary)*
- **State:** Indiana
- **In office:** January 29, 2018 – January 20, 2021
- **President:** Donald Trump
- **Notes:** Served for roughly 3 years, covering most of 2018–2020 and into early 2021 after Tom Price resigned in September 2017. He stepped down at the end of Trump's term, citing concerns about the Capitol riots on January 6, 2021. He was confirmed by the Senate on January 24, 2018 (55–43). He served as chairman of the White House Coronavirus Task Force early in the pandemic before it was replaced by Vice President Mike Pence.

---

### 2. **Norris Cochran** *(Acting Secretary)*
- **State:** Florida
- **In office:** January 20 – March 19, 2021
- **President:** Joe Biden
- **Notes:** A brief acting tenure of just **~7 weeks**, occurring during the transition from the Trump to Biden administration. Cochran, then Deputy Secretary, assumed the role when Azar formally stepped down effective January 20, 2021, until outgoing/interim arrangements and finally Xavier Becerra's confirmation concluded the transition on March 19, 2021.

---

### 3. **Xavier Becerra** *(25th Secretary)*
- **State:** California
- **In office:** March 19, 2021 – January 20, 2025
- **President:** Joe Biden
- **Notes:** Served for nearly **3 years and 10 months**, covering all of 2021, 2022, 2023, and all of 2024. He was the first Latino to serve as HHS Secretary. Confirmed by the Senate on March 18, 2021 (66–33). Became widely known for leading the federal COVID-19 vaccine rollout and overseeing major policy debates including abortion access, mental health, and opioid crises. His tenure continued through the entirety of your requested window (2018–2024).

---

### Summary Table

| Secretary / Status | Start Date | End Date | Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Alex Azar** (Confirmed) | Jan 29, 2018 | Jan 20, 2021 | ~3 years | Left after Trump term ended, citing Capitol riots |
| **Norris Cochran** (Acting) | Jan 20, 2021 | Mar 19, 2021 | ~7 weeks | Brief interim during transition |
| **Xavier Becerra** (Confirmed) | Mar 19, 2021 | Dec 31, 2024 | >3 years | Continued uninterrupted through entire window; left only Jan 20, 2025 |

---

**Key observations:**
- Only **one acting** secretary occurred within your window: Norris Cochran (briefly, in early 2021).
- Despite significant political upheaval (Trump → Biden transition, major policy debates, and controversies), **only two official secretaries** held the position continuously from 2018 through 2024: **Alex Azar** (through Jan 2021) and **Xavier Becerra** (from March 2021 onward).

The **United States secretary of health and human services** is the head of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services"), and serves as the principal advisor to the [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on health matters. The secretary is a member of the [United States Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cabinet "United States Cabinet"). [Robert F. Kennedy Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_F._Kennedy_Jr. "Robert F. Kennedy Jr.") is the incumbent secretary of health and human services, having held the position since February 13, 2025.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-2)

The office was formerly known as the secretary of health, education, and welfare. In 1980, the [Department of Health, Education, and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") was renamed to Department of Health and Human Services, and its education functions and [Rehabilitation Services Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehabilitation_Services_Administration "Rehabilitation Services Administration") were transferred to the new [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-3) [Patricia Roberts Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patricia_Roberts_Harris "Patricia Roberts Harris") headed the department before and after it was renamed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-4)

Nominations to the office are referred to the [Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor,_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions") and the [United States Senate Committee on Finance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Finance "United States Senate Committee on Finance"), which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-5) before confirmation is considered by the full [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"). The secretary of health and human services is a [level I position in the Executive Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Schedule#Level_I "Executive Schedule"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-6) thus earning a salary of [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Dollar "US Dollar")250,600, as of January 2025.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-Salary-7)

## Duties

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png/250px-Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health%2C_Education%2C_and_Welfare.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_Secretary_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare.png)The flag of the secretary of health, education, and welfare, the predecessor to the current office

The duties of the secretary revolve around human conditions and concerns in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). This includes advising the [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") on matters of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), [welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_security "Social security"), and income security programs. The secretary strives to administer the Department of Health and Human Services to carry out approved programs and make the public aware of the objectives of the department.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-8)

The [Department of Health, Education and Welfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health,_Education,_and_Welfare "United States Department of Health, Education, and Welfare") (HEW) was reorganized into a [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education") and a [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS).

The Department of Health and Human Services oversees 11 agencies including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA), [Centers for Disease Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control "Centers for Disease Control") (CDC), [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health") (NIH), [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") (ACF) and [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-9)

## Line of succession

The line of succession for the secretary of health and human services is as follows:[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services#cite_note-11)

1. [Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Deputy Secretary of Health and Human Services").
2. General Counsel of the Department of Health and Human Services
3. Assistant Secretary for Administration
4. [Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assistant_Secretary_for_Planning_and_Evaluation "Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation")
5. Administrator of the [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services")
6. [Commissioner of Food and Drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_Food_and_Drugs "Commissioner of Food and Drugs")
7. Director of the [National Institutes of Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institutes_of_Health "National Institutes of Health")
8. Assistant Secretary for [Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families")
9. Other assistant secretaries (following in the order they took the oath of office)
  1. [Assistant Secretary for Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Assistant_Secretary_for_Health "United States Assistant Secretary for Health")
  2. [Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Assistant_Secretary_for_Preparedness_and_Response "Office of the Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response")
  3. Assistant Secretary for Legislation
  4. Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs
  5. Assistant Secretary for Financial Resources
  6. Assistant Secretary for [Aging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_on_Aging "Administration on Aging")
10. Director of the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention")
11. Director, Region 4 ([Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"))

**Alex Michael Azar II** ([/ˈeɪzɑːr/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born June 17, 1967) is an American attorney, businessman, lobbyist, and former pharmaceutical executive who served as the 24th [U.S. secretary of health and human services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services") from 2018 to 2021. He was also chairman of the [White House Coronavirus Task Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Coronavirus_Task_Force "White House Coronavirus Task Force") from its inception in January 29, 2020 to February 26, 2020, when he was replaced by Vice President [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence").

In 2021, he was appointed a senior executive in residence at the [Miami Herbert Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Herbert_Business_School "Miami Herbert Business School") at the [University of Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Miami "University of Miami").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-FloridaPol21-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-MiamiAzar22-2)

From 2012 to 2017, Azar was [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_(corporate_title) "President (corporate title)") of the U.S. division of [Eli Lilly and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Lilly_and_Company "Eli Lilly and Company"), a major [drug company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_industry "Pharmaceutical industry"), and a member of the [board of directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") of the [Biotechnology Innovation Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology_Innovation_Organization "Biotechnology Innovation Organization"), a large [pharmaceutical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical "Pharmaceutical") [trade association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_association "Trade association").

Azar served as general counsel of the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Resources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS) from 2001 to 2005. On July 22, 2005, he was confirmed as the deputy secretary of health and human services; he served in that capacity until his January 2007 resignation.

## Early life and education

Azar was born on June 17, 1967, in [Johnstown, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnstown,_Pennsylvania "Johnstown, Pennsylvania"), the son of Lynda (Zarisky) and Alex Michael Azar Sr.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-4) His father is a retired [ophthalmologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ophthalmologist "Ophthalmologist") who practiced ophthalmology in [Salisbury, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury,_Maryland "Salisbury, Maryland"), for more than 30 years, and taught at [Johns Hopkins Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_Hospital "Johns Hopkins Hospital"). His grandfather emigrated from [Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanon "Lebanon") in the early 20th century. The family originates from [Amioun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amioun "Amioun").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whois-6)

Azar attended [Parkside High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkside_High_School "Parkside High School") in [Salisbury, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury,_Maryland "Salisbury, Maryland"), where he graduated in 1985. He received a [B.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree *[summa cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_honors "Latin honors")* in [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government "Government") and [economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") from [Dartmouth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College") in 1988. He belonged to the [Kappa Kappa Kappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kappa_Pi_Kappa "Kappa Pi Kappa") fraternity. He earned a [J.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juris_Doctor "Juris Doctor") degree from [Yale Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Law_School "Yale Law School") in 1991, where he served as a member of the executive committee of the *[Yale Law Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Law_Journal "Yale Law Journal")*.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-HHS06-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-ABA05-8)

## Career

### Law career

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Starr%2C_Kavanaugh%2C_and_Azar.jpg/250px-Starr%2C_Kavanaugh%2C_and_Azar.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Starr,_Kavanaugh,_and_Azar.jpg)Azar (on right) with [Ken Starr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Starr "Ken Starr") and [Brett Kavanaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Kavanaugh "Brett Kavanaugh") in the 1990s

After law school, from 1991 to 1992, Azar served as a [law clerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk") for Judge [Alex Kozinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Kozinski "Alex Kozinski") of the [United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Ninth_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit"). Azar left after six weeks, and was replaced in Kozinski's chambers by [Brett Kavanaugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Kavanaugh "Brett Kavanaugh").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-9) Azar subsequently clerked for the remainder of the term for Judge [J. Michael Luttig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Michael_Luttig "J. Michael Luttig") of the [United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Fourth_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit"). From 1992 to 1993, he served as a [law clerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_clerk "Law clerk") for Associate Justice [Antonin Scalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonin_Scalia "Antonin Scalia") of the [United States Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Supreme_Court "United States Supreme Court").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-10)

From 1994 to 1996, he served as an associate independent counsel for [Ken Starr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Starr "Ken Starr") in the [United States Office of the Independent Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_the_Independent_Counsel "United States Office of the Independent Counsel"), where he worked on the first two years of the investigation into the [Whitewater controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitewater_controversy "Whitewater controversy").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-LA_Times_1994-09-13-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-12) At the time of Azar's appointment, he was working as an associate in Starr's law firm.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-LA_Times_1994-09-13-11)

Between 1996 and 2001, Azar worked for [Wiley Rein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiley_Rein "Wiley Rein"), a [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), law firm, where he achieved partner status.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-speakerbio-13)

### Health and Human Services

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Alex_Azar_official_photo.jpg/250px-Alex_Azar_official_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alex_Azar_official_photo.jpg)Azar's official HHS deputy secretary portrait in August 2005

On August 3, 2001, Azar was confirmed as general counsel of the [United States Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-15) George W. Bush's first HHS secretary, [Tommy Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Thompson "Tommy Thompson"), said Azar played an important role in responding to the [2001 anthrax attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_anthrax_attacks "2001 anthrax attacks"), ensuring there was a vaccine ready for [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox"), and dealing with outbreaks of [SARS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS "SARS") and [influenza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influenza "Influenza").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whois-6) On July 22, 2005, Azar was confirmed as the deputy secretary of Health and Human Services.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-17) He was twice confirmed unanimously by the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate").

Working under Secretary [Mike Leavitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Leavitt "Mike Leavitt"), Deputy Azar supervised the operation of HHS, which would grow to an annual budget of over $1 trillion by 2017 when he was appointed secretary. Azar led the development and approval of HHS regulations, led U.S. government efforts to encourage worldwide pharmaceutical and medical device innovation, and was in charge of the HHS response to an initiative implemented by President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") to improve government performance.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whois-6) Azar resigned in January 2007.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-18)

### Eli Lilly and Company

In June 2007, Azar was hired by [Eli Lilly and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Lilly_and_Company "Eli Lilly and Company") chief executive officer [Sidney Taurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidney_Taurel "Sidney Taurel") to be the company's top [lobbyist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying "Lobbying") and [spokesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spokesperson "Spokesperson") as its senior vice president of corporate affairs and communications.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whois-6)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-investigation-19)

In April 2009, Azar became vice president of Lilly's U.S. Managed Healthcare Services organization and its [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico") affiliate.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-changes-20) In 2009, the company paid $1.415 billion to settle criminal charges regarding its promotion of [antipsychotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antipsychotic "Antipsychotic") drug Zyprexa ([olanzapine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olanzapine "Olanzapine")) for [off-label uses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-label_use "Off-label use") between 1999 and 2005.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-investigation-19)

Effective January 1, 2012, Azar became president of Lilly USA, LLC, the largest division of Eli Lilly and Company, and was responsible for the company's entire operations in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-changes-20) Prices for drugs rose substantially under Azar's leadership, including the tripling of the cost of the company's top-selling [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin") drug. Also under Azar's watch, Eli Lilly was one of three companies accused in a class-action lawsuit of exploiting the drug pricing system to increase profits for insulin. Eli Lilly was also fined in Mexico for colluding on the price of insulin.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-friend-22)

In connection with the position, Azar served on the board of directors of the [Biotechnology Innovation Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biotechnology_Innovation_Organization "Biotechnology Innovation Organization"), a [pharmaceutical lobby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_lobby "Pharmaceutical lobby").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-picks-23)

In January 2017, Azar resigned from Eli Lilly "to pursue other career opportunities" as a result of a company reorganization.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-24) He also resigned from the board of directors of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization. In his last year at the corporation he earned $2 million.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-25)

## U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services (2018–2021)

### Nomination and confirmation

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/President_Donald_Trump_and_Vice_President_Mike_Pence_with_Alex_Azar.jpg/250px-President_Donald_Trump_and_Vice_President_Mike_Pence_with_Alex_Azar.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:POTD-January-30-2018-2.jpg)Azar and his family with [President Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and [Vice President Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") in the [Oval Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oval_Office "Oval Office") shortly after being sworn in as [U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services") in January 2018

On November 13, 2017, President Trump announced via [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") that he would nominate Azar to be the next [secretary of health and human services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Secretary of Health and Human Services").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-picks-23)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-nominates-26)

Many health care advocates raised concerns about the nomination, citing Azar's track record of raising drug prices and his opposition to [Obamacare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-27) Critics noted that Azar approved a tripling of the price of insulin while vice president of Managed Healthcare Services of Eli Lilly.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-insulin-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-29) Speaking in favor of his nomination were two former U.S. Senate majority leaders, Democrat [Tom Daschle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Daschle "Tom Daschle") and Republican [Bill Frist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Frist "Bill Frist"). Both those endorsers were affiliated with the [Bipartisan Policy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipartisan_Policy_Center "Bipartisan Policy Center"), a Washington, D.C., think-tank which receives support from Eli Lilly.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-30)

In spite of objections, his nomination was relatively smooth. Azar was confirmed on January 24, 2018, with a 55–43 vote.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-31) with most Democrats opposed. Voting against him, Oregon senator [Ron Wyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Wyden "Ron Wyden"), ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee, said that while Azar was at Eli Lilly, he "never, not one time, signed off on a decrease in the price of a drug."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-32) Senator [Bernie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Sanders "Bernie Sanders") said in a press release, "The nomination of Alex Azar, the former head of Eli Lilly's U.S. operations, shows that Trump was never serious about his promise to stop the pharmaceutical industry from 'getting away with murder'." "The last thing we need is to put a pharmaceutical executive in charge of the Department of Health and Human Services." During that tenure, Eli Lilly was fined for colluding to maintain high drug costs in Mexico.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-insulin-28)

Azar had additionally consulted with numerous other biopharmaceutical and health insurance corporations regarding government policy, product access, sales and marketing, pricing, reimbursement, and distribution.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-insulin-28) He was confirmed by the Senate on January 24, 2018, and sworn in by Vice President Pence on January 29, 2018.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-Mangan20180129-33)

From March to December 2018, Azar sat on the [Federal Commission on School Safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Commission_on_School_Safety "Federal Commission on School Safety").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-34)

Azar had prolonged disputes with [Seema Verma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seema_Verma "Seema Verma"), who was Trump's administrator of the [Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_&_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services") (CMS).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-35) She accused Azar and his HHS predecessor, [Tom Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Price_(American_politician) "Tom Price (American politician)"), of sexist management; an inquiry by a former Trump HHS official, Heather Flick, concluded that Azar had not discriminated.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-37) Azar was widely reported to spar with his subordinates,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-38) leading to criticism of his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic response.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-39)

On January 20, 2021, immediately after the end of the Trump administration, China [sanctioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_sanctions "Chinese sanctions") Azar and other Trump administration officials. The sanctioned people cannot travel to China and cannot do business with China.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-41) President Biden's National Security Council called the sanctions "unproductive and cynical."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-PompeoSanctioned-42)

### Healthcare policy

#### Security Strategy

As Secretary of Health, Azar presided over the release of the Trump administration's [National Biodefense Strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Biodefense_Strategy "National Biodefense Strategy") in 2018 and the Global Health Security Strategy in 2019.

#### Affordable Care Act

Azar was an opponent of the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act"), also known as Obamacare. and predicted in 2017, "There will be a piece of legislation passes this year that is called the repeal of Obamacare. I don't know what's going to be in the substance of it, but there will be a piece of legislation that says that."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-nominates-26) Also regarding the ACA, Azar said the Department of Health and Human Services has latitude to "make it work a little better".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-friend-22)

#### Abortion

Azar opposes [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion"). In a written response to Senator [Patty Murray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patty_Murray "Patty Murray") regarding future HHS policy, he said, "The mission of HHS is to enhance the health and well-being of all Americans, and this includes the unborn."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-43)

#### Regulations

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/President_Trump_Hosts_a_Listening_Session_%2849118848461%29.jpg/250px-President_Trump_Hosts_a_Listening_Session_%2849118848461%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Trump_Hosts_a_Listening_Session_(49118848461).jpg)[President Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), [Kellyanne Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kellyanne_Conway "Kellyanne Conway"), Senator [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney"), and Azar during a [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") listening session on youth [vaping and electronic cigarette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_cigarette "Electronic cigarette") use

According to *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*, Azar differed with his predecessor, [Tom Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Price_(American_politician) "Tom Price (American politician)"), in his approach to regulations. Writing in May 2018, the *Times* reported, "in a sharp break from his predecessor – and from most Trump cabinet secretaries – he seems to be relishing the chance to write new regulations, rather than just crossing out Obama-era ones."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-44)

### COVID-19

#### Outbreak

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849483221341%29.jpg/250px-White_House_Press_Briefing_%2849483221341%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:White_House_Press_Briefing_(49483221341).jpg)Azar speaks to the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") press corps on [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 in the United States") in March 2020[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/President_Trump_Signs_the_Congressional_Funding_Bill_for_Coronavirus_Response_%2849627907646%29.jpg/250px-President_Trump_Signs_the_Congressional_Funding_Bill_for_Coronavirus_Response_%2849627907646%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Trump_Signs_the_Congressional_Funding_Bill_for_Coronavirus_Response_(49627907646).jpg)President Trump, with Azar, signs the [Coronavirus Preparedness and Response Supplemental Appropriations Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_Preparedness_and_Response_Supplemental_Appropriations_Act,_2020 "Coronavirus Preparedness and Response Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2020") into law in March 2020

Azar learned about the [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") threat on January 3, 2020.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-wsj-covid-45) Azar informed associates that he had alerted Trump on January 18, 2020, regarding the potential danger from [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"),[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-wsj-covid-45) but that the president thought he was being "alarmist" as Azar struggled to get Trump's attention to focus on the issue.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-China-46) Despite Azar's warnings, four days later, Trump announced, "We have it totally under control. It's one person coming in from [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-47) On January 28, 2020, Azar stated that the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") had no plan to declare a public health emergency as the [COVID-19 virus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Severe_acute_respiratory_syndrome_coronavirus_2 "Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2") spread in China. He asserted that the risk to Americans was minimal, but admitted that authorities in 30 states were monitoring potential cases and added that he would not "hesitate at all to invoke any authorities I need to, to ensure we're taking all steps to protect the American people, but I'll do it when it's appropriate." U.S. senator [Rick Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Scott "Rick Scott"), U.S. representative [Vern Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vern_Buchanan "Vern Buchanan"), and other Republicans demanded that a public health emergency be declared as a means of budgeting necessary [federal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") funding to deal with the potential pandemic.

At the time, Azar said, there were just five confirmed cases in the U.S., there was no known person-to-person transmission, and every confirmed U.S. victim had traveled to [Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan"), China, the outbreak's place of origin. "This is potentially a very serious public health threat, but at this time Americans should not worry about their own safety", Azar said. At that point, the disease had killed at least 106 people in China, with more than 4,500 cases confirmed.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-48) On January 29, 2020, Azar told Trump that the [COVID-19 epidemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_epidemic "COVID-19 epidemic") was under control.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-wsj-covid-45)

However, two days later, on January 31, 2020, Azar declared a public health emergency.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-49) The determination that a public health emergency existed from COVID-19 was renewed in April, July, and October 2020, and in January 2021.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-50)

On February 27, U.S. representative [Jimmy Gomez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Gomez "Jimmy Gomez") of California revealed that he had been contacted by a whistleblower from the [Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS) who had been dispatched to deal with the arrivals of travelers exposed to the coronavirus. There were allegations made that those sent from the HHS to California quarantine sites lacked both sufficient protective clothing and the training necessary to prepare them to deal with the contagion, though they were working alongside CDC personnel who wore adequate protective gear.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whistleblower-51) The whistleblower also said that professionals raising concerns about the unsafe practices were subjected to retaliation.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whistleblower-51)

Azar responded to the issues raised by Gomez, saying, "Urgency does not compensate for violating isolation and quarantine protocols" and adding, "I'd want to know the full facts and would take appropriate remedial measures."[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whistleblower-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-52) Azar insisted that careful protocols were being observed by all CDC employees.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whistleblower-51)

On February 28, 2020, [United States Senate Finance Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Finance_Committee "United States Senate Finance Committee") ranking member [Ron Wyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Wyden "Ron Wyden") wrote Azar to ask why employees of the HHS [Administration for Children and Families](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administration_for_Children_and_Families "Administration for Children and Families") were involuntarily dispatched to California to meet with quarantined travelers despite lacking expertise in the field and lacking proper information, equipment, and training. Wyden also asked why said employees were not cleared to ensure that they had not become carriers of the disease before they were returned to their home stations.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-53)

On April 25, 2020, multiple media outlets reported that the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") was weighing a plan to oust Azar due to frustrations over his response to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-57)

The following day, President Trump tweeted that such reports were "[fake news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fake_news "Fake news")" and that he has no plans to replace Azar.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-60)

Azar picked [Brian Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Harrison_(Texas_politician) "Brian Harrison (Texas politician)"), a 37-year old former [Labradoodle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labradoodle "Labradoodle") breeder who had no formal education in public health or related fields, but who had worked in the HHS for six years, as HHS's main coordinator for the government's response to the coronavirus.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-61)

#### Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

As secretary of health and human services, Azar was responsible for the [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Disease_Control_and_Prevention "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention") (CDC), a key institution in charge of containing contagious diseases. On January 28, 2020, Azar requested that the Chinese government allow a CDC expert team into their country to help them learn more about the virus. Referring to the SARS epidemic 17 years earlier, Azar said, "I can say that the posture of the Chinese government levels of cooperation and interaction with us is completely different from what we experienced in 2003 and I want to commend them for such assistance." The [World Health Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Health_Organization "World Health Organization") had already agreed to supply international experts to visit China "as soon as possible". Seventy-three possible cases were being monitored in the U.S. Simultaneously, the CDC had ramped up coronavirus screenings of travelers coming into the U.S. at 20 airports. Azar said it might be possible to ban any travelers arriving from China, and all options had to be considered. "Diseases are not terribly good at respecting borders", he added.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-62)

#### Congressional testimony and requests for funding

On February 25, 2020, Azar appeared before the Senate Appropriations Committee to testify on the danger of and responses to the pandemic. Louisiana Republican senator [John Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kennedy_(Louisiana_politician) "John Kennedy (Louisiana politician)") asked both Azar and [Chad Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chad_Wolf "Chad Wolf") about the fatality rate in victims. Azar said that the fatality rate of seasonal influenza was about 0.1%, and that the fatality rate of [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") was estimated at between 1% and 2%; however, Azar added that the latter figure was uncertain because there might be many mild coronavirus cases yet unreported.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-63)

Chad Wolf said that the fatality rate for COVID-19 was between 1.5% and 2%, and said incorrectly that the fatality rate for influenza over the last 10 years in America was similar (about 2%).[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-65) Kennedy was unhappy with the briefing, saying afterward, "I thought a lot of the briefing was bullshit ... They would answer the question but dodge, bob, and weave. I understand there's a lot they don't know. I get that. But they need to answer the questions straight up. They all talk about a task force, a committee – a committee's not going to solve this problem."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-66)

Trump's officials tried to allay concerns that their request for $2.5 billion was insufficient to address the epidemic. Some Republicans joined Democrats in criticizing the funds requested and found transparency lacking with regard to a coherent strategy to contain the virus. Another Republican, Senate Appropriations Committee chairman [Richard Shelby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Shelby "Richard Shelby") of Alabama, told Azar: "If you lowball something like this, you'll pay for it later."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-Politico-67)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-cuts-69) Pennsylvania Democratic congressman [Brendan Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Boyle "Brendan Boyle") asked Azar how he could defend "draconian cuts" in the CDC budget "at the same time we are facing a unique worldwide health crisis."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-cuts-69)

Two years earlier, a coalition of global health organizations opposed Trump's plans to reduce the CDC's operations in 39 of 49 countries in which it had been helping to rapidly identify and suppress outbreaks of diseases. The coalition wrote to Azar, contending, "These programs are essential to our national defense".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-cuts-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-demotion-70) In 2018, National Security Advisor [John Bolton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bolton "John Bolton") dismantled the task force charged with responsibility for planning and response to epidemics. The team's leader, Rear Admiral [Timothy Ziemer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Ziemer "Timothy Ziemer"), was the leader of the anti-malarial efforts under presidents [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") and [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-cuts-69) White House Homeland Security Advisor [Tom Bossert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Bossert "Tom Bossert"), who had advocated a comprehensive biodefense strategy against both pandemics and potential biological attacks, departed from the White House on the same day Bolton arrived.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-cuts-69)

#### HHS purchase of 500,000 doses of remdesivir

On June 29, 2020, it was announced that the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "United States Department of Health and Human Services") (HHS) had agreed to buy 500,000 [remdesivir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remdesivir "Remdesivir") treatment courses. The announcement mentioned that each five-day course of remdesivir for treatment of a patient with [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") would cost at least $2,340.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-US-HHS-500K-remdesivir-71) HHS Secretary Alex Azar was quoted, and had said (in a press release) that "To the extent possible, we want to ensure that any American patient who needs remdesivir can get it."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-US-HHS-500K-remdesivir-71)

#### Testing

Further information: [COVID-19 testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_testing "COVID-19 testing")

On March 2, 2020, Azar was criticized for unpreparedness that may have accelerated the spread of the virus. Some critics focused on the lack of definitive testing of those who might be spreading the virus. China had tested over one million people, while the CDC had tested fewer than 500 and its results had been undermined by problems with accuracy and potential contamination. There was substantial internal feuding with regard to formulation of policy at HHS and the CDC.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-72)

#### Vaccine

Azar argued that the pharmaceutical industry was best poised to discover, manufacture, and market a vaccine for coronavirus. When asked about the cost of vaccines, Azar responded that the price might be high, but that an important vaccine would be created even if many Americans could not afford it.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-73)

[https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/87/Operation_Warp_Speed_Leaders_Hold_Briefing_on_Vaccine.webm/Operation_Warp_Speed_Leaders_Hold_Briefing_on_Vaccine.webm.240p.vp9.webm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/8/87/Operation_Warp_Speed_Leaders_Hold_Briefing_on_Vaccine.webm/Operation_Warp_Speed_Leaders_Hold_Briefing_on_Vaccine.webm.240p.vp9.webm)

Azar holds a briefing on the release of the [COVID-19 vaccine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_vaccine "COVID-19 vaccine") in January 2021[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-hhs.gov-74)

On January 12, 2021, Azar announced[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-hhs.gov-74) that HHS would be releasing remaining stockpiles of vaccine to states; however, at the time of the announcement, all stockpiles had already been exhausted.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-Kristen_Holmes_and_Sara_Murray-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-Stanley-Becker-76) This was met with confusion and anger from various governors.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-77)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-78)

#### Rule ban

In September 2020, Azar forbade health agencies, including the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration"), from making new rules on foods, medicines, medical devices, or other products, including vaccines, without his permission. His memo to the agencies declared that such power "is reserved to the Secretary." Health advocates said that the memo raised questions about political meddling and might slow down decision-making. It was unclear if the change would affect work on [COVID-19 vaccines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_vaccine "COVID-19 vaccine").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-79)

### Taiwan visit

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/20200810%E8%94%A1%E8%8B%B1%E6%96%87%E7%B8%BD%E7%B5%B1%E6%8E%A5%E8%A6%8B%E3%80%8C%E7%BE%8E%E5%9C%8B%E8%A1%9B%E7%94%9F%E9%83%A8%E9%95%B7%E9%98%BF%E6%9C%AD%E7%88%BE%E8%A8%AA%E5%95%8F%E5%9C%98%E3%80%8D4.jpg/250px-20200810%E8%94%A1%E8%8B%B1%E6%96%87%E7%B8%BD%E7%B5%B1%E6%8E%A5%E8%A6%8B%E3%80%8C%E7%BE%8E%E5%9C%8B%E8%A1%9B%E7%94%9F%E9%83%A8%E9%95%B7%E9%98%BF%E6%9C%AD%E7%88%BE%E8%A8%AA%E5%95%8F%E5%9C%98%E3%80%8D4.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20200810蔡英文總統接見「美國衛生部長阿札爾訪問團」4.jpg)Azar with [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Taiwan "President of Taiwan") [Tsai Ing-wen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsai_Ing-wen "Tsai Ing-wen") in August 2020

On August 9, 2020, Azar was the first member of the [U.S. Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_United_States "Cabinet of the United States") to visit [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") in six years.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-81)

Azar said the trip was to convey Trump's support for Taiwan's leadership in global health, reiterate U.S. support for Taiwan, and cooperate on global health and health safety issues.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-82) The next day, he signed a [memorandum of understanding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorandum_of_understanding "Memorandum of understanding") on Medical and Health Cooperation in [Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei "Taipei").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-84)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-85)

On January 20, 2021, the [Government of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") imposed sanctions against Azar, outgoing U.S. secretary of state [Mike Pompeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pompeo "Mike Pompeo"), former under secretary of state [Keith J. Krach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_J._Krach "Keith J. Krach"), outgoing U.S. ambassador to the United Nations [Kelly Craft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Craft "Kelly Craft"), and 24 other former Trump officials.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-86) Biden's National Security Council called the sanctions "unproductive and cynical."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-PompeoSanctioned-42)

### Resignation letter

On January 12, 2021, Azar submitted his letter of resignation, effective January 20. Although he announced it as the customary resignation that all political appointees submit at the end of a presidential term,[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-87) the resignation letter included commentary urging President Trump to promote a peaceful and orderly transition to the Biden presidency in view of the [storming of the U.S. Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_storming_of_the_United_States_Capitol "2021 storming of the United States Capitol") the previous week.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-89)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-90)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-91) After leaving government service in 2021, Azar returned to the private sector, focusing on healthcare consulting and advisory roles.

### COVID-19 lawsuit

In 2022, Azar was co-defendant in a civil rights suit in the [Ninth Circuit Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Appeals_for_the_Ninth_Circuit "United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit") seeking to compel the CDC to publish mortality statistics in which COVID-19 was unequivocally the primary cause of death.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-92)

## Personal life

Azar is an [Antiochian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiochian_Orthodox_Christian_Archdiocese_of_North_America "Antiochian Orthodox Christian Archdiocese of North America") Christian and former [Episcopalian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-94) He is of [Lebanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lebanese_people "Lebanese people"), Ukrainian, English, and Swiss descent.

Before his nomination, he lived in [Indianapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis "Indianapolis") with his wife and two children.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-Mangan20180129-33)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-95)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-speakerbio-13) Azar served for two years on the board of [HMS Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Holdings "HMS Holdings").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-96) He is currently on the board of the American Council on Germany, where he is chairman of the Strategic Planning Committee, and the [Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis_Symphony_Orchestra "Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra").

He has previously served on the board of directors of the [Healthcare Leadership Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthcare_Leadership_Council "Healthcare Leadership Council"), where he was treasurer; the [National Association of Manufacturers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Manufacturers "National Association of Manufacturers"); and the [Indianapolis International Airport Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis_Airport_Authority "Indianapolis Airport Authority"), where he was chairman of the Human Resources Committee.

In 2020, Azar revealed he has [celiac disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coeliac_disease "Coeliac disease") while discussing a U.S. Food and Drug Administration rule related to [gluten-free](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gluten-free_diet "Gluten-free diet") labeling for [fermented foods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermented_foods "Fermented foods").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-97)

### Politics

Azar is a [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") and has contributed to the campaigns of [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence"), [Mitch McConnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_McConnell "Mitch McConnell"), [Orrin Hatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orrin_Hatch "Orrin Hatch"), [Lamar Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamar_Alexander "Lamar Alexander"), [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush "Jeb Bush"), and Donald Trump, according to [OpenSecrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenSecrets "OpenSecrets").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Azar#cite_note-whois-6)

resposta:
Os **8 times brasileiros** que se classificaram para a Copa Libertadores de 2021 foram:

| Time | Classificação |
|------|---------------|
| **Palmeiras** | Campeão da Libertadores 2020 (vaga automática) |
| **Flamengo** | Campeão do Campeonato Brasileiro de 2020 |
| **Internacional** | Vice-campeão do Brasileiro de 2020 |
| **Atlético-MG** | 3º colocado do Brasileiro de 2020 |
| **São Paulo** | 4º colocado do Brasileiro de 2020 |
| **Fluminense** | 5º colocado do Brasileiro de 2020 (ganhou vaga por ter conquistado a Copa do Brasil, já que o Palmeiras, também finalista, estava classificado) |
| **Grêmio** | 6º colocado do Brasileiro de 2020 (entraram pelas fases preliminares, via Copa do Brasil) |
| **Santos** | 8º colocado do Brasileiro de 2020 (entraram pela segunda fase) |

**Como funcionou a divisão:**

- **8 vagas diretas para a fase de grupos:** Palmeiras, Flamengo, Internacional, Atlético-MG, São Paulo, Fluminense (vaga obtida via Copa do Brasil) e Grêmio.
- **Duas vagas extras** (via Copa do Brasil/Sul-Americana): Santos entrou pela 2ª fase, e o Grêmio chegou à fase de grupos após eliminar o Ayacucho (Peru) na segunda fase.

No torneio, **apenas o Grupo F não teve representante brasileiro**. Os brasileiros se distribuíram pelos Grupos A, B, C, D, E, G e H — e o **Palmeiras venceu a competição**, conquistando seu tricampeonato ao bater o Flamengo na final.

A **[Copa Libertadores da América](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América "Copa Libertadores da América") de [2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021 "2021")**, oficialmente **CONMEBOL Libertadores 2021**, foi a 62.ª edição da competição de futebol realizada anualmente pela [Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Sul-Americana_de_Futebol "Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol") (CONMEBOL). Participam clubes das dez associações sul-americanas.

Em 13 de maio de 2021, o conselho da CONMEBOL de maneira virtual definiu a cidade de [Montevidéu](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevidéu "Montevidéu"), no Uruguai, como sede das finais da Libertadores e da [Copa Sul-Americana](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2021 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2021").[[2]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-2) Com isso, o [Estádio Centenario](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Centenario "Estádio Centenario") passou por um processo de modernização pela [CONMEBOL](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederação_Sul-Americana_de_Futebol "Confederação Sul-Americana de Futebol") e contou com a presença de público, já que a maioria da população do Brasil e do Uruguai estava vacinada contra a [COVID-19](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19").[[3]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-3)

O [Palmeiras](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") conquistou seu terceiro título da competição – o segundo seguido, já que conquistou a [Copa Libertadores da América de 2020](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2020 "Copa Libertadores da América de 2020") – ao vencer o [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo") na [final](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2021 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021") por 2–1.[[4]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-4) Com isso, ganhou o direito de representar a CONMEBOL na [Copa do Mundo de Clubes da FIFA de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_do_Mundo_de_Clubes_da_FIFA_de_2021 "Copa do Mundo de Clubes da FIFA de 2021"), nos [Emirados Árabes Unidos](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirados_Árabes_Unidos "Emirados Árabes Unidos"), de enfrentar o campeão da [Copa Sul-Americana de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Sul-Americana_de_2021 "Copa Sul-Americana de 2021") na [Recopa Sul-Americana de 2022](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recopa_Sul-Americana_de_2022 "Recopa Sul-Americana de 2022"), assim como se classificou automaticamente para a fase de grupos da [Copa Libertadores da América de 2022](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2022 "Copa Libertadores da América de 2022"). Ademais, em 14 de março de 2023 a FIFA confirmou a participação do campeão do torneio no [Mundial de Clubes FIFA de 2025](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundial_de_Clubes_FIFA_de_2025 "Mundial de Clubes FIFA de 2025"), nos Estados Unidos.

## Equipes classificadas

As seguintes 47 equipes das 10 federações filiadas à CONMEBOL se qualificaram para o torneio:

- Campeão da Copa Libertadores da América de 2020
- Campeão da Copa Sul-Americana de 2020
- Brasil: 7 vagas
- Argentina: 6 vagas
- Demais associações: 4 vagas cada

A fase de entrada é determinada da seguinte maneira:

- **Fase de grupos: 28 equipes**
  - Campeão da Copa Libertadores de 2020
  - Campeão da Copa Sul-Americana de 2020
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 1 a 5 da Argentina e do Brasil
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 1 e 2 de todas as outras associações.
- **Segunda fase: 13 equipes**
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 6 e 7 do Brasil
  - Equipe que qualificou para a vaga 6 da Argentina
  - Equipes qualificadas para as vagas 3 e 4 do Chile e Colômbia
  - Equipes qualificadas para a vaga 3 de todas as outras associações.
- **Primeira fase: 6 equipes**
  - Equipes que se qualificaram para a vaga 4 da Bolívia, Equador, Paraguai, Peru, Uruguai e Venezuela

### Primeira fase

A primeira fase foi disputada por seis equipes provenientes de Bolívia, Equador, Paraguai, Peru, Uruguai e Venezuela, em partidas eliminatórias de ida e volta. Em caso de empate no placar agregado, a [regra do gol fora de casa](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regra_do_gol_fora_de_casa "Regra do gol fora de casa") seria considerada e, persistindo a igualdade, a vaga seria definida na [disputa por pênaltis](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disputa_por_pênaltis "Disputa por pênaltis"). Os confrontos desta fase foram definidos através de sorteio.[[9]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-sorteio2-9)

### Terceira fase

A terceira fase foi disputada pelas oito equipes vencedoras da fase anterior, em partidas eliminatórias de ida e volta. ## Fase final

Após a conclusão da fase de grupos, um sorteio realizado em 1 de junho definiu o chaveamento das equipes classificadas a partir das oitavas de final até a final.[[12]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-sorteio-12)

As equipes que finalizaram em primeiro lugar na fase de grupos (pote 1 no sorteio) enfrentaram as equipes que finalizaram em segundo lugar (pote 2), podendo ser sorteadas equipes de um mesmo país ou que integraram o mesmo grupo na fase anterior. A pontuação obtida na fase de grupos serve para a definição dos mandos de campo até a semifinal, com as equipes melhores posicionadas sempre realizando o jogo de volta como local (numerados de 1 a 16).[[11]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-regulam-11)[[12]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-sorteio-12)

### Final

Ver artigo principal: [Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Final_da_Copa_Libertadores_da_América_de_2021 "Final da Copa Libertadores da América de 2021")

O Palmeiras defendeu o título de então campeão e derrotou o Flamengo por 2–1 após a [prorrogação](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prorrogação "Prorrogação"). Após abrir o marcador com gol do meia [Raphael Veiga](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphael_Veiga "Raphael Veiga") no primeiro tempo, a equipe paulista sofreu o empate no segundo tempo, com gol marcado pelo atacante [Gabriel](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Barbosa "Gabriel Barbosa"), fazendo com que o jogo terminasse no tempo normal em 1–1. Na prorrogação, o atacante [Deyverson](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deyverson "Deyverson") fez o gol do título, após tomar a bola do meia [Andreas Pereira](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Pereira "Andreas Pereira"), levando o Palmeiras ao tricampeonato da competição.[[13]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-13)

- 27 de novembro **[Palmeiras](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociedade_Esportiva_Palmeiras "Sociedade Esportiva Palmeiras") [Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasil "Brasil")** **2 – 1 ([pro](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prorrogação "Prorrogação"))** **[Brasil](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brasil "Brasil") [Flamengo](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clube_de_Regatas_do_Flamengo "Clube de Regatas do Flamengo")** [Estádio Centenario](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estádio_Centenario "Estádio Centenario"), [Montevidéu](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevidéu "Montevidéu")
- 17:00 ([UTC−3](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−3 "UTC−3")) [Raphael Veiga](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raphael_Veiga "Raphael Veiga") Gol marcado aos 5 minutos de jogo 5'
 [Deyverson](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deyverson "Deyverson") Gol marcado aos 95 minutos de jogo 95' [Relatório](https://www.conmebol.com/analisis-del-partido?season=2021&competition=420&match=2253364) [Gabriel](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Barbosa "Gabriel Barbosa") Gol marcado aos 72 minutos de jogo 72' **Público:** 45 000[[14]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-público_2021-14)

Valores totais

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Palmeiras_x_Flamengo_-_Libertadores_-_Final_-_Torcida.jpg/250px-Palmeiras_x_Flamengo_-_Libertadores_-_Final_-_Torcida.jpg?utm_source=pt.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ficheiro:Palmeiras_x_Flamengo_-_Libertadores_-_Final_-_Torcida.jpg)Torcida do Palmeiras na arquibancada do Estádio Centenário

Durante a fase de grupos, cada clube recebeu cerca de 1 milhão de [dólares](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dólar "Dólar"), sendo que os dois finalistas arrecadaram aproximadamente 16 milhões de [reais](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_(moeda_brasileira) "Real (moeda brasileira)"). Ao avançar para as oitavas, cada equipe garantiu mais US$ 1,05 milhão. Nas quartas de final, a premiação da Libertadores 2021 foi de US$ 1,5 milhão e, por fim, mais US$ 2 milhões na semifinal. O título do torneio ainda garante mais US$ 15 milhões, enquanto o segundo colocado fica com US$ 6 milhões.[[15]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-premiação-15)

No total, o campeão arrecada pouco mais de R$ 120 milhões, enquanto o segundo colocado fica com cerca de R$ 73 milhões de premiação.[[15]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-premiação-15)

## Notas

- **a.** [**^**](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#ref_Anone) Não definido no momento do sorteio.

- **URU** [**^**](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#ref_URUnone) Como o Campeonato Uruguaio de 2020 ainda estava em disputa com o início da Copa Libertadores de 2021, a [Associação Uruguaia de Futebol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asociación_Uruguaya_de_Fútbol "Asociación Uruguaya de Fútbol") (AUF) resolveu estabelecer datas de corte para determinar suas equipes classificadas. Conforme essas datas, as vagas foram oferecidas pela AUF após a quinta rodada do Torneio Clausura, na ordem em que as equipes estavam posicionadas na tabela da temporada.[[21]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-21) A primeira data de corte foi em 7 de fevereiro, e a equipe que aceitou a vaga (Liverpool) se classificou como "Uruguai 4" (Nacional, [Montevideo City Torque](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_City_Torque "Montevideo City Torque"), [Peñarol](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Peñarol "Club Atlético Peñarol") e [Rentistas](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Atlético_Rentistas "Club Atlético Rentistas") abriram mão). A segunda data foi em 21 de fevereiro, com a equipe que aceitou a vaga (Montevideo Wanderers) se classificando como "Uruguai 3" (Nacional, Montevideo City Torque e Peñarol abriram mão). Caso o campeonato ainda não tivesse sido concluído até 11 de abril, esta seria a última data de corte com as equipes se classificando como "Uruguai 1" e "Uruguai 2".[[22]](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores_da_Am%C3%A9rica_de_2021#cite_note-22)

# Oito clubes brasileiros garantem vaga na Libertadores; veja os classificados

Com o fim do Campeonato Brasileiro de 2020, [conquistado pelo Flamengo](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/esporte/2021/02/25/flamengo-supera-inter-e-vence-brasileirao-pelo-segundo-ano-consecutivo), foram definidos também os clubes classificados para a Copa Libertadores e para a Copa Sul-Americana.

Flamengo, Internacional, Atlético-MG e São Paulo, os quatro primeiros colocados do Brasileirão, além do Palmeiras, [atual campeão do torneio continental](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/esporte/2021/01/30/aos-53-do-segundo-tempo-palmeiras-marca-e-e-bicampeao-da-libertadores), já estão garantidos na fase de grupos da competição.

Fluminense e Grêmio – 5º e 6º no Campeonato Brasileiro, respectivamenete – também garantiram, ao menos, uma vaga na fase preliminar da Libertadores.

Um dos dois, no entanto, passará automaticamente para a fase de grupos depois da final da Copa do Brasil enquanto o outro enfrentará o Ayacucho, do Peru, na fase 2 da competição.

Isso porque a final da Copa do Brasil – cujo campeão garante uma vaga na Libertadores – [será entre o próprio Grêmio e o Palmeiras](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/esporte/2020/12/31/finalistas-copa-do-brasil), já classificado para a Libertadores por ser o atual campeão continental.

Se o time paulista ganhar, a vaga direta fica com o tricolor carioca. Se o Grêmio vencer, então será o próprio tricolor gaúcho que escapará das fases prévias da Libertadores.

Oitavo colocado no Brasileiro, o Santos também garantiu uma vaga na Libertadores. O clube entrará na segunda fase e jogará com o Deportivo Lara, da Venezuela.

Os confrontos prévios da Libertadores foram definidos no começo de fevereiro pela Conmebol. Já os grupos serão sorteados em 9 de abril. Os confrontos da competição começam em 20 de abril.

Veja todos os clubes brasileiros que jogarão a Libertadores em 2021:

- Flamengo (fase de grupos)
- Internacional (fase de grupos)
- Atlético-MG (fase de grupos)
- São Paulo (fase de grupos)
- Palmeiras (fase de grupos)
- Fluminense (fase de grupos/fase 2)
- Grêmio (fase de grupos/fase 2)
- Santos (fase de 2)

## Copa Sul-Americana

O fim do [Brasileirão 2020](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/tudo-sobre/campeonato-brasileiro) também confirmou os seis clubes brasileiros que disputarão a Copa Sul-Americana.

Neste ano, do 9º ao 14º colocado no torneio nacional garantiram vaga para a competição. São eles, respectivamente: Athletico-PR, Bragantino, Ceará, Corinthians, Atlético-GO e Bahia.
